questions.stem: For linear search over an array of $n$ elements, what are the best-case and worst-case numbers of comparisons?

options.text: Best 1, worst $n$
Best 1, worst $\log_2 n$
Best $n/2$, worst $n$
Best 1, worst $n/2$

questions.explanation: The best case is one comparison, when the target is the first element examined. The worst case is $n$ comparisons, occurring both when the target is last and when it is absent — and absence is the more important of the two, because a correct algorithm must inspect every element before it can report "not found". The average for a successful search on a uniformly distributed target is about $(n+1)/2$, which is still $\Theta(n)$.

distractorRationale.b: Quotes the binary search bound, which requires a sorted array
distractorRationale.c: Confuses the average case with the best case
distractorRationale.d: Reports the average as the worst case; an unsuccessful search alone forces $n$ comparisons

questions.stem: What precondition must hold before binary search may be applied, and what happens if it is violated?

options.text: The array must be sorted; otherwise the algorithm may report "not found" for a value that is present
The array length must be a power of two; otherwise the midpoint calculation fails
The array must contain no duplicates; otherwise the algorithm loops forever
The array must be stored in a linked list; otherwise halving is impossible

questions.explanation: Binary search discards half the range after one comparison, and the only justification for discarding it is the sortedness assumption: if the target is less than the midpoint value, sortedness guarantees it cannot lie to the right. On unsorted input the algorithm still terminates in $O(\log n)$ steps but its answer is unreliable — a silent wrong answer, which is worse than a slow one.

distractorRationale.b: Integer division handles any length; a power of two is not required
distractorRationale.c: Duplicates are fine — the search simply finds some matching index rather than a specified one
distractorRationale.d: The reverse is true: binary search *requires* random access, which a linked list cannot provide

questions.stem: Binary search runs on the sorted array [11, 22, 33, 44, 55, 66, 77, 88, 99] with indices 0 to 8, using `mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2)`. How many elements are examined while searching for 33? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Probe 1: lo = 0, hi = 8, mid = 4, value 55. Since $33 < 55$, set hi = 3. Probe 2: mid = floor(3/2) = 1, value 22. Since $33 > 22$, set lo = 2. Probe 3: mid = floor(5/2) = 2, value 33 — found. Three elements are examined, consistent with the worst-case bound $\lfloor \log_2 9 \rfloor + 1 = 4$.

questions.stem: What is the maximum number of elements binary search examines in a sorted array of 1,000,000 elements? Give a number only.
questions.explanation: Each probe at most halves the candidate range, so after $k$ probes the range has size at most $n/2^k$. The search terminates once that reaches 0, needing $k = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor + 1$ probes. Here $2^{19} = 524{,}288 < 10^6 \le 2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$, so 20 probes suffice. Compare 1,000,000 for linear search — a factor of 50,000.

questions.stem: You must perform $k$ searches on a static array of $n$ elements. When is sorting once and then using binary search preferable to performing $k$ linear searches?

options.text: Always, because $O(\log n)$ beats $O(n)$
Never, because the sort costs more than any number of searches
When $k$ is large enough that $n \log n + k \log n < kn$ — roughly when $k$ exceeds $\log n$
Only when $k$ equals 1, so the sort cost is incurred once

questions.explanation: The two totals are $\Theta(kn)$ for repeated linear search and $\Theta(n \log n + k \log n)$ for sort-then-bisect. Since $k \log n$ is dominated by $kn$, the comparison reduces to $n \log n$ against $kn$, so sorting pays off once $k \gtrsim \log n$. For $n = 10^6$ that threshold is about 20 searches — very low, which is why static lookup tables are almost always kept sorted or indexed.

distractorRationale.a: Ignores the one-off $\Theta(n \log n)$ preprocessing, which dominates when $k$ is small; for a single search a linear scan is genuinely cheaper
distractorRationale.b: The sort is amortised over all $k$ searches, so its cost per search falls as $k$ grows
distractorRationale.d: Inverts the argument — $k = 1$ is precisely the case where sorting is *not* worthwhile

questions.stem: A binary search implementation computes `mid = (lo + hi) / 2` using fixed-width signed integers. Why is `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` preferred?

options.text: It produces a different midpoint that converges faster
It avoids overflow: for large `lo` and `hi` the sum can exceed the integer range, whereas the difference cannot
It avoids division, which is slower than subtraction
It is required when the array length is odd

questions.explanation: Both expressions are algebraically equal, but `lo + hi` can exceed the maximum representable integer when both indices are large — the sum silently wraps negative and the resulting index is out of bounds. Since `hi >= lo`, the quantity `hi - lo` is bounded by the array length and cannot overflow. This bug survived in the JDK's `Arrays.binarySearch` for nine years, which is a useful reminder that a correct algorithm and a correct implementation are different achievements.

distractorRationale.a: For non-overflowing values the two expressions yield the identical midpoint
distractorRationale.c: Both forms perform one division; the change is about range, not arithmetic cost
distractorRationale.d: Integer division handles odd lengths identically in both forms

questions.stem: Binary search applied to a **sorted singly linked list** of $n$ nodes still runs in $O(\log n)$ time.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Binary search performs $O(\log n)$ *comparisons*, but reaching each midpoint requires random access. On a linked list the midpoint of a range must be reached by traversing links, which costs $\Theta(n)$ in total across the halvings, so the running time is $\Theta(n)$ — no better than a linear scan, and with more code. This is why sorted sequences that must support bisection are stored contiguously or in a balanced tree, which provides the halving structurally.

questions.stem: Which recurrence describes binary search, and what does it solve to?

options.text: $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1)$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(\log n)$
$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(1)$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n)$
$T(n) = T(n-1) + \Theta(1)$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n)$
$T(n) = 2T(n/2) + \Theta(n)$, giving $T(n) = \Theta(n \log n)$

questions.explanation: Binary search makes one constant-time comparison and then recurses on **one** half of the range, so the recurrence is $T(n) = T(n/2) + \Theta(1)$. Unrolling it gives a sum of $\Theta(1)$ terms over $\log_2 n$ levels, so $T(n) = \Theta(\log n)$. The single recursive call is the essential feature: recursing on both halves would visit every element.

distractorRationale.b: Two subproblems would mean examining both halves, which is a full traversal rather than a search
distractorRationale.c: That is the recurrence for linear search, which shrinks the range by one element
distractorRationale.d: That is the merge sort recurrence, where both halves are solved and merged in linear time
